analysis.evidence: In זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה בְּרָאָם, ‘male and female he created them,’ זָכָר is paired with נְקֵבָה ‘female’ to identify the sexes of those created.
analysis.morphology: Adjective, masculine singular absolute, used substantivally, with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה בְּרָאָם means “male and female he created them.” The pairing with זָכָר ‘male’ establishes the sense ‘female’, and the shared name אָדָם ‘humankind’ identifies the pair as human.
analysis.morphology: The conjunction וּ ‘and’ is prefixed to a feminine singular absolute common noun.
analysis.sense: A female, here a female human.

analysis.evidence: זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה (“male and female”) identifies whom God created. The suffix ־ם refers to both, as does אֹתָם (“them”) in the following clause, “and he blessed them.”
analysis.morphology: Qal perfect, third person masculine singular, with a third person masculine plural direct-object suffix.

analysis.evidence: The subject is God, and אֹתָם (“them”) refers to the male and female he created. Genesis 5:2 recalls Genesis 1:27–28, where God blesses the human pair and tells them to be fruitful and multiply.
analysis.morphology: Piel wayyiqtol, third person masculine singular, with prefixed וַ־ and no suffix
analysis.sense: to bless living creatures with fruitfulness

draft.change: Add Genesis 5:2 to the evidence for the existing object-pronoun sense in et.
draft.definition: The suffixed direct-object marker expresses the person or people acted on.
draft.evidence: Genesis 5:2 expresses the same object first by a suffix on בְּרָאָם and then by the separate form אֹתָם after וַיְבָרֶךְ.

analysis.evidence: In וַיְבָרֶךְ אֹתָם, “and he blessed them,” the suffix refers back to זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה, “male and female.” The preceding בְּרָאָם, “he created them,” has the same plural object.
analysis.morphology: Direct-object marker in its suffixed form אֹת־ with the third-person masculine plural pronominal suffix ־ָם.
analysis.sense: Carries a pronominal suffix that supplies the verb’s direct object.

analysis.evidence: אֶת marks שְׁמָם (“their name”) as the direct object, and אָדָם gives the name God assigned to the male and female together.
analysis.morphology: Qal wayyiqtol, third person masculine singular, with prefixed וַ.

analysis.evidence: In וַיִּקְרָא אֶת שְׁמָם אָדָם, “he called their name Adam,” אֶת marks שְׁמָם (“their name”) as the direct object of וַיִּקְרָא. The possessive suffix makes שְׁמָם definite, and אָדָם gives the name assigned.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew direct-object particle without a prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: The plural suffix in שְׁמָם (“their name”) refers to the male and female whom God created and blessed. אָדָם is the shared designation he gives them.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular absolute common noun, used collectively.

analysis.evidence: בְּיוֹם is followed by הִבָּרְאָם, a Niphal infinitive construct meaning “their being created.” Together they specify when God named them אָדָם, “on the day they were created.”
analysis.morphology: Prefixed preposition בְּ + masculine singular construct noun יוֹם
analysis.sense: the time when; on the day that

analysis.evidence: The suffix refers to the male and female. The opening בְּרָאָם means “he created them,” and בְּיוֹם הִבָּרְאָם describes the same event in the passive, “on the day they were created.”
analysis.morphology: Niphal infinitive construct with the third-person masculine plural suffix ־ָם as its subject.
